Environmental Ed Day 10 12 The Art Of Getting Closer To Nature While Getting Farther Away From The Nearest Flush Toliet

Oct 19, 2010 • Janice Cotcher

I did it. I survived to tell the tale of the time I went camping in mid-October in Saskatchewan. I’ve camped in cold weather before but never near winter camping. I knew as long as I was prepared, I would not have any problems. The purpose of the camping weekend was to learn about food sovereignty, to build a community within our class and (of course) learn wilderness skills.

When we arrived on Friday, there were wind gusts up to 70 km/h. We had a terrible time getting the fly on top of my tent. Unlike some of my classmates, I knew to pegs at a 45 degree angle towards the tent so once it was up, the tent stayed firm.

I had a hard time sleeping Friday night with all the wind. I brought 3 sleeping bags so I was warm enough but the wind was just too loud. I put in my ear plugs but then the tent wall hitting my head kept me awake.

On Saturday, as part of learning about food sovereignty, we worked at the Green Ranch. The Green Ranch is a small plot intensive farm near Osage, SK. They supply restaurants in Regina like The Fainting Goat and The Willow as well as sell at the Regina Farmers’ Market. Seeing how much they produce in such a small space really got me thinking about how I will use any land I may own in the future.

In Tudor times, a lawn become a status symbol for the the aristocracy and gentry. [Source: Lawn, Wikipedia] It was to say “I have so much land, can use this space for leisure.” These were owners with massive parcels of land. Working at the Green Ranch got me thinking, what could I produce in a garden the size of my backyard? We are so blessed with many parks in Regina so isn’t it a waste to have a backyard full of grass? Our family eats on the patio in the back but we rarely use the yard in the back. We have a front yard with grass and a park less than half a block away. It definitely makes me see suburban land usage different.

On Saturday afternoon, the winds died down significantly. I was exhausted from having so little sleep the night before so I went to bed early. You could certainly tell that it went down to -6C that night because my tent was covered in frost when I woke up. I had to pack up the tent still covered in frost (I dried it out at home).

Today in class as we debriefed the weekend, the topic of being prepared came up. No matter how much you prepare, there will always be something you forget. It was also mentioned that those students are going to learn will learn regardless if you mess up or not. Sort of bittersweet when you think of about it.

We also got talking about the time and effort needed to take classes on field trips. I think that is the main reason that many classes don’t go on field trips although these are the experiences that students remember the most. How much work am I willing to do for my class to have a valuable learning experience? Sometimes the school cannot provide the money that will be needed for an activity. Am I ready to say no to the activity? Or am I prepared to use my own money to give my students a learning experience outside the classroom?
